items.title: World Bank's Banga: Availability of capital 'not really an issue' as AI demand drives up borrowing costs
items.summary: World Bank President Ajay Banga came on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Oct. 27, 2026.
items.body: World Bank President Ajay Banga said on Tuesday that capital remained available despite concerns of artificial intelligence sending interest rates higher. Banga said the World Bank mobilized $112 billion last year, around three times the amount recorded three years prior. He said investors may be concerned about circular financing and the business model tied to AI. But Banga told CNBC that emerging markets are not running into the same hesitancy because the investments focus more on infrastructure like bridges and roads. These countries also look at smaller-scale uses of AI, according to Banga. Banga said developed counterparts look to funding to support large use cases, which he described as the "exact opposite" need. The World Bank leader also said that the private capital it oversees does not go to governments.

items.title: Robinhood shares fall 4% as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses
items.summary: Robinhood's third-quarter revenue met expectations, fueled by the company's expansion into options, predictions markets and other financial services.
items.body: Robinhood shares fell 4% in after-hours trading as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets. Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year. Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting the focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity. Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform.

items.title: I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40 - it's hard
items.summary: People earning from £380 a month to £150,000 a year tell the BBC what they want to see in this year's Budget.
items.body: Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs". BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget. If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice . Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living. She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills.

items.title: Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor
items.summary: From tackling the youth jobs crisis to repairing Brexit’s economic damage, John Healey has his work cut out for him John Healey will deliver his first budget on Wednesday as UK households and businesses come under pressure from the unfolding economic shock caused by the war in…
items.body: John Healey will deliver his first budget on Wednesday as UK households and businesses come under pressure from the unfolding economic shock caused by the war in the Middle East. Against a febrile backdrop in global markets, the chancellor is facing a delicate balancing act to provide “breathing space” measures to ease the cost of living crisis while increasing growth and sticking to the fiscal rules. Healey will also flesh out Andy Burnham’s pledge to deliver “ good growth in every postcode ”, with measures to hand local leaders more money and power. At the spring statement, Healey’s immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, left herself £23.6bn of “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which require day-to-day spending to be matched by receipts by the end of this parliament.

items.title: October 2026 euro area bank lending survey
items.body: According to the October 2026 bank lending survey (BLS), euro area banks reported a further net tightening of credit standards – banks’ internal guidelines or loan approval criteria – for loans or credit lines to enterprises in the third quarter of 2026 (net percentage of 9% of banks; Chart 1). Banks reported unchanged credit standards for loans to households for house purchase (net percentage of 0%) and a further net tightening for consumer credit and other lending to households (net percentage of 14%). For firms, the net tightening surpassed the expectations reported by banks in the previous survey round (5%). Heightened risk perceptions and banks’ reduced risk tolerance remained the main drivers of tighter credit standards, with some banks reporting increasing pressure as a result of geopolitical uncertainty and energy developments.

items.title: China’s energy supply chain is withstanding test of Middle East war, expert says
items.summary: China’s energy security, now buttressed by internal resilience, has withstood a difficult test from the protracted war in the Middle East, says the head of a global energy industry body. “China has domestic production, it has developed a diversification policy and there is also…
items.body: China’s energy security, now buttressed by internal resilience, has withstood a difficult test from the protracted war in the Middle East, says the head of a global energy industry body. “China has domestic production, it has developed a diversification policy and there is also the possibility to switch around different types of energy,” Andrea Stegher, president of the International Gas Union (IGU), told the South China Morning Post on Tuesday. Stegher said the world’s second-largest economy had energy supply chains more complete than some others, with Beijing balancing a combination of domestic and overseas sources. “China’s domestic [natural gas] production is more than double Norway’s, and we consider Norway from the European standpoint being very large … China also has [natural gas] pipelines coming from Central Asia, like from Turkmenistan,” he explained.

items.title: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
items.summary: Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the e-commerce giant's sprawling business operations under CEO Andy Jassy.
items.body: Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools. The memo , which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI. "We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice." Under CEO Andy Jassy , Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations.

items.title: Fed rate hikes are coming, but not this week: CNBC survey
items.summary: The CNBC Fed Survey shows that 93% of respondent expect a pause at the Federal Reserve meeting taking place this week.
items.body: The Federal Reserve has considerable work to do. But it's not going to do it in October. That's the key finding in CNBC's latest Fed Survey of 30 fund managers, strategists and economists, which showed that 93% expect a pause at the Fed meeting taking place this week and 76% anticipate a rate hike at its next meeting in December. And more than half say the Fed will hike next year by an average of about two rate hikes. "Their hesitancy to raise rates is unfathomable after an extended period of monetary and fiscal generosity, with nominal GDP running 6-8%, and when the leading indicators of inflation are uniformly warm to hot,'' said Richard Bernstein, global head of macro investing at Janus Henderson Investors. A plurality of 40% say the Fed must slow growth below potential to solve the inflation problem .

items.title: AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.
items.summary: Credit markets will be closely watching updates from Oracle and other hyperscalers later this week. What to expect.
items.body: Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming. Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively. Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms ' plans for a $95 billion stock offering , announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off. Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team.

items.title: Homes across UK to get low- or no-interest loans to fund solar panels and heat pumps
items.summary: Government-backed Warm Home Loans scheme to help households cut energy bills by hundreds of pounds Households across the UK can now cut their energy bills by hundreds of pounds a year at no upfront cost by applying for interest-free or “low-interest” loans to fund upgrades such…
items.body: Households across the UK can now cut their energy bills by hundreds of pounds a year at no upfront cost by applying for interest-free or “low-interest” loans to fund upgrades such as heat pumps, batteries and solar panels. The government-backed Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, could mean thousands more households are able to access low-carbon energy alternative technologies, thanks to loans ranging from £7,500 to up £35,000. Energy suppliers including British Gas and E.On have partnered with lenders from Tandem Bank and Homeserve respectively to offer the loans directly to customers at a discounted rate compared with those offered by high street lenders.

items.title: China hands former regulator suspended death sentence over US$65m bribery charge
items.summary: A former high-ranking official with China’s securities regulator was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve on Tuesday over bribery charges, as Beijing continues its sweeping anti-corruption campaign. Wang Huimin, who served as a member of the Communist Party committee of…
items.body: A former high-ranking official with China’s securities regulator was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve on Tuesday over bribery charges, as Beijing continues its sweeping anti-corruption campaign. Wang Huimin, who served as a member of the Communist Party committee of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) from 2014 to 2019, was found to have taken more than 436 million yuan (US$65 million) in bribes. “The amount involved was especially large and caused especially heavy losses to the interests of the state and the people, warranting the death penalty,” the Chengdu Intermediate People’s Court said in its verdict. Wang was appointed to oversee discipline at the CSRC by China’s top anti-corruption watchdog, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, but later became the target of an investigation himself.

items.title: Trump administration may let more Russian diesel onto market, energy secretary tells CNBC
items.summary: The diesel volumes in the Trump-Putin deal won't materially lower prices because the shipments are small compared to total demand, analysts say.
items.body: The U.S. may allow more diesel fuel from Russia onto the global market depending on Moscow's behavior, Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC in an interview Tuesday. Wright framed the Trump administration's suspension of U.S. sanctions against Russian diesel exports earlier this month as "an incentive" for Moscow to end the war in Ukraine. It will help with fuel supplies on the margin, he said. The Russian-flagged tanker Talisman is expected to arrive on the U.S. East Coast on Nov. 9, according to the ship-tracking platform MarineTraffic. Another tanker, the Leruo, has departed Russia en route to the "Atlantic Coast" without explicitly declaring its destination as the U.S. More tankers with Russian diesel could "quite possibly" set sail under the U.S.

items.title: Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar
items.summary: As crypto evolves past its trading roots, and global markets shift to 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure.
items.body: Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD , strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management. The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year . It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients. "Utility is what moves stablecoins forward.

items.title: Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned
items.summary: Plans to switch to digital landlines by January could leave remote areas of the UK vulnerable, MPs say.
items.body: Plans to switch off the UK's traditional landline phone network could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency, MPs have warned. Landline operators aim to complete the switch to an internet-based network instead of copper-wire cables by the end of January next year. The government and operators say the move to digital landlines will offer a more reliable service. But MPs representing remote areas of the UK urged security minister Dan Jarvis to ensure that scrapping the copper-wire network did not make their communities more vulnerable in a storm or other emergency. Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and continues to work in a power cut.

items.title: Bottled water and tinned food sales surge after UK government issues emergency stockpile advice
items.summary: Retailers also report jump in purchases of wind-up radios and torches to deal with extreme weather and cyber-attacks Sales of tinned foods, bottled water, wind-up radios and torches have surged after the UK government advised households to prepare for emergencies . Retailers…
items.body: Sales of tinned foods, bottled water, wind-up radios and torches have surged after the UK government advised households to prepare for emergencies . Retailers have reported a jump in sales of items linked to preparation for emergencies such as extreme weather or cyber-attacks. The Be Ready campaign was launched last week with the aim of persuading households to lay in supplies to last 72 hours. Maplin said sales of torches had almost quadrupled and sales of power banks and radios had doubled. One brand of emergency wind-up radio sold out on Friday. The specialist technology retailer said sales would have been higher but it was low on stock, particularly for power banks after a summer of heatwaves and the fallout from the Iran war. Home security camera sales were up 130%.

items.title: Football star Kylian Mbappe faces huge China backlash over ‘unacceptable’ remark
items.summary: French football superstar Kylian Mbappe has issued an apology after an “ill-judged” comment about China sparked intense backlash on social media and led a string of major Chinese brands to cut ties with him. After a video began circulating widely online that appeared to show the…
items.body: French football superstar Kylian Mbappe has issued an apology after an “ill-judged” comment about China sparked intense backlash on social media and led a string of major Chinese brands to cut ties with him. After a video began circulating widely online that appeared to show the France and Real Madrid striker making a controversial remark about former Chinese leader Mao Zedong, several Chinese firms including the dairy giant Mengniu announced they were pulling out of deals with him on Tuesday. “Mengniu firmly opposes and has zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people,” Mengniu said in a statement, as the firm confirmed it was immediately terminating “all partnerships” with Mbappe.

items.title: Speaker Mike Johnson calls election-transfer concerns ‘absurd’
items.summary: Democrats and voting rights groups have raised concerns that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans could challenge election results if they lose.
items.body: U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson , R-La., committed Tuesday to a peaceful postelection transfer of power, calling concerns that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans could contest the results if Democrats win control of Congress "absurd." "We're going to follow the Constitution," Johnson said in Orangeburg, New York during a campaign stop with Republican Rep. Mike Lawler one week before the Nov. 3 midterm election . "The Constitution says when a state certifies the election of members of Congress, then they're administered the oath. That's what I'll be doing on Jan. 3 to everybody who's there," Johnson said in response to a question from MS NOW. "I may not like some of those outcomes, but that's our system," he said.

items.title: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiar
items.summary: Donald Trump heads into the US midterm elections with an issue similar to his political foe Joe Biden.
items.body: The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is. It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them. Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs. Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high . The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies. The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market.

items.title: Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’
items.summary: Administrator BTG says 738,144 firms struggling as calls grow for more support for private sector in budget Business live – latest updates The number of UK businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, as pressure grows on the chancellor to…
items.body: The number of UK businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, as pressure grows on the chancellor to provide more support to the private sector in Wednesday’s budget . There were 738,144 businesses in “significant” financial distress in the third quarter of this year, up 1.6% compared with the same period last year, according to BTG. That is the highest level since the administrator’s closely watched “red flag” report began in 2004. The UK’s support services, construction and real estate sectors were among the most vulnerable, with the highest numbers of businesses in significant distress – at 118,695, 108,340 and 99,908 respectively. The hospitality industry was hardest hit this year, with a 5% rise in the number of bars and restaurants in distress to 18,866.

items.title: Chart: Anthropic's cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company
items.summary: Anthropic's cash pile of $131.7 billion is more than every non-bank U.S. company except for Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet.
items.body: The nearly 6-year-old artificial intelligence lab disclosed on Monday in an S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it had $112.4 billion in cash, plus another $19.3 billion in short-term investments, as of June 30. Anthropic's total of $131.7 billion surpasses every non-bank U.S. company, except for Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet , according to data compiled by CNBC and S&P Capital IQ. As of midyear, Anthropic had more cash than Amazon , SpaceX , Meta and Microsoft . It had more than Nvidia and Apple combined. Depending on how much the company raises in its initial public offering — and reports suggest it could top $100 billion — Anthropic could bump its hoard to more than $230 billion in cash.

items.title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
items.summary: Figures obtained by BBC Newsnight show large spikes in sales of torches, radios and power banks.
items.body: Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight. The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend. The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event. Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks. The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.

items.title: UK officials discussing options including free movement with EU ahead of summit
items.summary: Business secretary says focus for November summit will be trade and youth mobility, but talks will also include ‘future options for relationship’ UK politics live – latest updates British officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could…
items.body: British officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could include a return to free movement, the business secretary has said while promising the British people “are the boss” when it comes to what the UK will accept. Jonathan Reynolds said the focus for British negotiations was the EU summit in November to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But he said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had made it clear he wanted to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc. “They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be. But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we’re going to make,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

items.title: Boeing says it won't significantly ramp up 737 Max production until late 2027
items.summary: Boeing is set to brief investors on its aircraft production outlook when it reports quarterly results before the market opens Tuesday.
items.body: Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production. CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month. Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected because of the wings production pace. "I know everybody wants us to go faster, but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday. "Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday.

items.title: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
items.summary: The France star had referred to the former Chinese leader as a "dictator" during an interview about memes.
items.body: Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands. Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao. The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football. "My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement. Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".

items.title: HSBC says ‘no pressure’ to move HQ out of UK despite prospect of higher bank taxes
items.summary: As John Healey’s budget decision looms, lender reports 32% rise in profits A top executive at HSBC has tried to quash speculation that the bank could move its headquarters out of the UK over tax increases expected to be announced in Wednesday’s budget. HSBC’s chief financial…
items.body: A top executive at HSBC has tried to quash speculation that the bank could move its headquarters out of the UK over tax increases expected to be announced in Wednesday’s budget. HSBC’s chief financial officer, Pam Kaur, said there was “no pressure”, particularly from shareholders in its cornerstone Hong Kong market, to shift out of London despite lobbyists warning higher tax bills could drive big banks’ business abroad. HSBC on Tuesday revealed a 32% rise in third-quarter profits to $9.6bn (£7.2bn), alongside plans to give $2.7bn to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. Lobby groups have for months warned that banks could shift business and jobs to rival hubs if threatened with higher bills, with the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, saying he could even scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if Britain became “hostile” to banks.

items.title: Polymarket faces renewed CFTC probe over U.S. access to offshore platform
items.summary: The federal agency had previously investigated whether Polymarket allowed U.S. users on to its offshore platform in 2024, but dropped the measures in July 2025.
items.body: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Polymarket violated a 2022 settlement meant to ban U.S. users from its offshore platform, according to a person familiar with the matter. The investigation is part of a broader probe the agency opened into Polymarket earlier this year, after a Wall Street Journal expose said Polymarket paid content creators to post videos showing simulated trades and fabricated wins on dummy versions of its website. The latest inquiry focuses on whether Polymarket previously broke the 2022 settlement, and is unrelated to the platform's present operations, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly.

items.title: Apple to replace iPhone Duos affected by screen problem
items.summary: Photos shared online showed faults appearing on the screens of Apple's first foldable device.
items.body: Apple has acknowledged some of its iPhone Duo handsets have developed problems with their screens, just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale. Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device , which has a starting price of £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK. Apple said it was aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement. The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, is an attempt to reinvigorate the brand's device range and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals. Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

items.title: ‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey film
items.summary: Tesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbuster Elon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”. Having criticised the…
items.body: Elon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”. Having criticised the hit movie in the summer, the tycoon said he would use Grok Imagine to make a “historically accurate” adaptation. The initial results have been released on X in the form of a seven-minute episode made in conjunction with Wonder Studios, a London-based startup. Musk had objected to Nolan’s casting choices – such as black actor Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy – and used the blockbuster as a vehicle for reciting his views on diversity, equity and inclusion. The Tesla tycoon had promised to make a “ full-length movie ” version of Homer’s poem before the year ends but is sticking to a film released in episodes. The first episode starts with Odysseus agonising over whether to join the Greek forces in their attempt to sack Troy.

items.title: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote
items.summary: Tens of thousands of Israelis are returning home to vote in a tight election.
items.body: An extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes. Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters , according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems. "While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.

items.body: Kylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga. The offending video shows Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photoshopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao. “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” Mbappé said in a statement in French, Chinese and English.

items.title: Fed expected to hold rates steady, but Warsh may point way to more hikes
items.summary: Markets overwhelmingly expect no change in benchmark interest rates following September's increase.
items.body: Federal Reserve officials enter this week's policy meeting amid a critical debate over what the central bank can, should and will do to address an inflation problem that shows no immediate sign of going away. When the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee does release its decision Wednesday, markets overwhelmingly expect no change in benchmark interest rates following September's quarter percentage point rate increase . Investors will be looking closely, though, for clues about future moves from policymakers, and Chairman Kevin Warsh in particular. Brett Ryan, senior U.S. economist at Deutsche Bank, said he'll be watching what Warsh will signal about future policy moves — something the Fed chairman has said he is highly reluctant to do as he seeks to move the central bank away from the "forward guidance" practice of most of the 21st century.

items.body: Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget at around 12:30 on Wednesday. The speech, which usually lasts about an hour, will be broadcast live on BBC iPlayer and on the BBC News website. He and Prime Minister Andy Burnham are hoping to give households "breathing space" amid the ongoing high cost of living. But Healey has also refused to rule out some tax increases to potentially pay for support he could distribute elsewhere. The government has run an unusually tight ship, preventing policies leaking out ahead of time, but here are the key measures expected. The Budget will contain more details on Burnham's planned Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property. items.body: T o the east of Oxford Circus, there is chaos. A steady stream of red London buses swing round the last junction before the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street begins. The streets are crammed with pedestrians, some squabbling over who poked whom with their umbrella first. It may be a wetter Monday morning than London’s mayor would have dreamed of, but Sadiq Khan hailed it a “momentous day”. Almost a kilometre of the capital’s most famous shopping street has now been pedestrianised, banishing the buses, bikes, taxis, e-scooters and pedicabs along with private cars.

items.title: How much is the minimum wage?
items.summary: What are the National Minimum Wage and the National Living Wage, and how much are they worth?
items.body: The rate for workers aged 21 and over is called the National Living Wage, while those aged 18 to 20 are paid the National Minimum Wage. A rise is expected in the Budget on Wednesday , with 18-20 year-olds seeing the same rise as over-20s. The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from £10.85 an hour to around £11.27. The level for 18-20 year-olds increasing at the same rate as over-20s is a break from recent efforts by the government to end the disparity in the minimum wage based on age. From 1 April 2026, workers over 21 on the National Living Wage are paid £12.71 an hour, 50p more than in 2025. For someone working full time (37.5 hours a week), that amounts to £24,784.50 a year - an increase of £900. The government said its goal is to eventually scrap this separate rate for 18 to 20-year-olds, and have one rate for all adults.

items.title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny | Nils Pratley
items.summary: A regulator to keep the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank on mission is starting to look essential Two winners in the budget are known already. They are the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, state-funded investment bodies that have rapidly…
items.body: T wo winners in the budget are known already. They are the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, state-funded investment bodies that have rapidly become central to the government’s growth strategy. The former chancellor Rachel Reeves handed extra slugs of capital to both and now John Healey is going further. The NWF will get another £15.4bn over the next half decade, on top of its existing £27.8bn, and there’ll be another £5bn for the BBB, which already has £25.6bn. Expect a fanfare about “over 100,000 jobs across the country to be created” via the extra capital for these so-called PuFins. The term means public financial institutions. They invest in private sector assets, either directly or through third-party funds, with the aim of making a profit for the taxpayer – or, at least, earning a return that matches or beats the government’s cost of borrowing.

items.title: Israel election puts Netanyahu’s wartime leadership on the line as Trump urges voters to return him to power
items.summary: Israeli voters will head to the polls to cast their votes in a general election on Tuesday.
items.body: Israeli voters will head to the polls Tuesday in an election with implications beyond the country’s borders. It is Israel’s first election since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, which killed around 1,200 people and saw more than 250 abducted. The Palestinian Ministry of Health says Israel’s subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,500 people . It is also the first vote since the U.S. and Israel began their joint war against Iran in February. With defense at the forefront of the debate for all the main contenders, tens of thousands of Israeli citizens are believed to have flown home to cast their votes in what is expected to be a tight-knit race. Israelis vote for parties rather than directly electing a prime minister, with the Knesset’s 120 seats allocated through proportional representation. Parties must win at least 3.25% of the national vote to enter parliament.

items.summary: The shelter has seen a "huge increase" in the number of cats it has taken in, compared to last year.
items.body: An animal charity has said the cost of caring for pets is among reasons for a "huge increase" in the number of cats and kittens being taken in by its centre. RSPCA Coventry and District Branch said it cared for 399 cats and kittens over the summer, which was 150 more than the same time last year. Emma Davies of the centre said: "We think a lot of that is down to rising costs," adding it included the cost of neutering pets, which in turn resulted in more kittens being born. Nationally, the RSPCA has warned of a "cat crisis" and said it is now caring for more felines than dogs, adding that the influxes have put pressure on its centres. The site in Coundon Wedge Drive, Coventry, is run independently to the national RSPCA and said it costs £40,000 a month to run the shelter.

items.title: My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hard | Polly Toynbee
items.summary: Bankers have barely begun to repay the billions they cost the country after 2008. In this PM they may have met their match Vibes matter. We live by how we feel – an idea that orthodox economics gets wrong and Andy Burnham’s first budget looks set to get right. This walking…
items.body: Vibes matter. We live by how we feel – an idea that orthodox economics gets wrong and Andy Burnham’s first budget looks set to get right. This walking good-vibes maestro is spreading a confetti of small good deeds. These may not shift the dial yet on 40 years of neoliberal economics, but they show the way he’s heading. Eyecatching everyday things – from capping bus fares to that small but resonant sum of £45 VAT on average off electricity bills – get people talking, alongside bigger plans for a national care service , electoral reform and a possible journey back to the EU . Though his first budget is billed as unradical, one tax rise stands out for its Burnham vibes. After years of no penalties, no apologies, no payback for their bailout from the crash they caused, banks face a tax rise . The Tories’ cuts to the bank levy and bank profits surcharge were left in place by Rachel Reeves.

items.body: I n John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism. Or will we? Capital gains tax equalised with income tax? Ruled out . A genuine wealth tax on those sitting on over £10m? Off the table . Even the briefed increase in the banking surcharge only takes us back to where it was until the Conservatives cut it in 2023. We can cross our fingers for trailed policies on supporting high streets, financial devolution and longer-term investment, but there is still more than a whiff of trickle-down economics in the air. Poll after poll shows that the British public overwhelmingly supports wealth taxes on the super-rich – including three in five Reform-leaning voters.

items.title: Margin debt growth slows sharply as stock market warning signs build
items.summary: Slowing margin-debt growth could signal growing risks for stocks.
items.body: The pace at which investors are borrowing money to invest in stocks has cooled substantially, raising concern that the stock market may be due for a fall. Recent FINRA data shows the annual growth in margin debt fell to 31.4% in September from 53.7% in May, Bank of America technical strategist Paul Ciana pointed out in a Friday note. Ciana warned that slowing borrowing momentum from extreme levels has been associated with previous market peaks. May's growth rate in 2026 was the fourth highest since 1998, according to a BofA analysis. The three higher extremes took place in 2000, 2007 and 2021 — all of which preceded stock market declines. Earlier this year, borrowing was increasing much faster than stocks were rising. Analysts view high borrowing levels as a contrarian signal, similar to bull-bear sentiment indicators.

The 23-year-old hopes it would give him the chance to put down roots after spending much of his childhood moving around because of his father's Army career. Further details of the government's proposed Your First Home scheme are expected in Wednesday's Budget, with ministers saying it could help first-time buyers purchase a property with a deposit as low as 2.5%. "I don't think I've ever stayed in one place for more than three years at a time, so it would be nice to actually have somewhere where I can stay," he said. items.title: Four takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filing
items.summary: The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards Anthropic has filed to go public on the US stock market, revealing for the first time the AI research lab’s financials and all…
items.body: Anthropic has filed to go public on the US stock market, revealing for the first time the AI research lab’s financials and all the risks – more than 90 pages of them – that might negatively affect its business. The company’s investor prospectus, released on Monday, veers from hyperbolic predictions about AI’s “incredible potential” to existential risks of the technology to the reality of its current business: explosive but incredibly expensive growth. The filing to US financial regulators, known as an S-1, provides the public’s first look at an audited version of Anthropic’s finances. Here’s what you need to know: Anthropic is making a lot of money. It’s also losing a lot of it. The five-year-old firm has been valued between $1.5 and $2tn by some investors but did not list a target valuation in its S-1. Founded in 2021, the company has seen explosive growth every year of its existence.

The community centre is in the heart of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's constituency, Makerfield, and they know all about budgeting here as it is run entirely by volunteers and has recently had to raise thousands of pounds for a new roof. items.body: Coca-Cola on Tuesday raised its full-year outlook for the third straight quarter, despite lackluster demand in its home market. For the full year, Coke now expects comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from its prior forecast of an increase in the range of 9% to 10%. The beverage giant also anticipates that its organic revenue will climb at least 5%, a slight increase from its previous outlook of approximately 5% growth. CEO Henrique Braun attributed the company's strong results to its "speed and discipline" despite the "uneven environment," he said on the company's earnings conference call. Looking ahead to 2027, the company expects consumer behavior to remain unchanged, CFO John Murphy said. In recent quarters, Braun and other executives have said North American shoppers are under pressure, stretched thin by inflation and economic uncertainty, and looking for value.

items.title: Britain’s fridge disposal crisis and what to do about it | Letters
items.summary: Readers respond to an article by Sam Wollaston about Norfolk’s fridge mountain Sam Wollaston ( What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain, 21 October ) highlights an urgent issue, but misses a key underlying driver: the reality of climate change and…
items.body: Sam Wollaston ( What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain, 21 October ) highlights an urgent issue, but misses a key underlying driver: the reality of climate change and increasingly hot UK summers. Many standard UK fridge-freezers are only built to normal (N) ambient climate classes, rated to operate in temperatures up to +32C. During recent heatwaves, indoor temperatures in many homes regularly exceed this limit. Even subtropical (ST) rated units fail when ambient temperatures push past 38C. When ambient limits are exceeded, cooling systems fail, leading to compressor breakdown, spoiled food and premature appliance disposal.

items.title: Super-rich get ‘double dividend’ from causes and costs of climate crisis, report finds
items.summary: Oxfam says investing by rich in disaster recovery widens inequality and gives incentive to delay climate action The world’s wealthiest people are not just profiting from the polluting causes of climate breakdown, they are also increasingly cashing in on the catastrophic…
items.body: The world’s wealthiest people are not just profiting from the polluting causes of climate breakdown, they are also increasingly cashing in on the catastrophic consequences, according to a study by Oxfam . The global equality organisation has found that the richest 0.1% of the world’s population are heavily invested in disaster preparedness, recovery and reconstruction – a market that is projected to grow from $70bn to $92bn a year by 2029. This gives the planet’s wealthiest and most powerful people a “double dividend” from the climate crisis and, more alarmingly, an incentive to delay or disrupt action to solve the problem, the NGO says. It also worsens global inequality as those least responsible for global heating end up having to pay those most responsible in terms of higher food prices, repairing homes damaged by extreme weather or relocating to other areas.

items.body: Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers. The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out. It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday. Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.

items.summary: Investigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plans The UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without any meetings with environmental groups, an investigation has found. The nonprofit…
items.body: The UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without any meetings with environmental groups, an investigation has found. The nonprofit organisation Spotlight on Corruption said a “considerable revolving door” shaped the government’s development of “AI growth zones”, a central plank of the former prime minister Keir Starmer’s AI and economic policy, with 38 ministers, senior civil servants and special advisers hired to positions in AI companies between July 2024 and September 2026. Meanwhile, even as top officials left government for jobs at OpenAI and Anthropic, government departments largely failed to engage meaningfully with stakeholders outside the technology industry.

items.title: Judge blasts prosecutors, refuses to sign new criminal complaint against ex-FBI officials
items.summary: Two ex-FBI officials were initially accused by the DOJ of lying when they testified to Congress in 2023 about their involvement in Hunter Biden investigations.
items.body: A judge on Tuesday sharply criticized federal prosecutors for failing to get judicial approval before filing a new criminal complaint overnight against two ex-FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about investigations of Hunter Biden . Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said he would not sign off on the new complaint, which added a charge of obstruction against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides in U.S. District Court in Washington. "I am not going to bless it as a superseding complaint," Faruqui said at a court hearing, after Floris' lawyers filed a motion arguing the new complaint was legally deficient and filed in bad faith. He told prosecutors that if they wanted to file a superseding complaint, a judge first would have to find probable cause that a crime had been committed, instead of sending him the complaint in the middle of the night and expecting him to sign it.

items.title: Landowners could scupper free Land Registry access plans, campaigners warn
items.summary: Proposed lifting of paywall would reveal who owns vast majority of land in England and Wales Plans by the government to give the public free access for the first time to information on who owns England’s land are at risk of being scuppered by landowners, campaigners have said.…
items.body: Plans by the government to give the public free access for the first time to information on who owns England’s land are at risk of being scuppered by landowners, campaigners have said. On Tuesday the government set out its proposals to lift the paywall on the Land Registry, arguing that opening it would help the UK build more houses, protect nature and improve strategic planning. The plans will be open to public consultation for eight weeks. The Guardian has previously revealed that there are internal rifts between the government and the Land Registry – an “arm’s length body” that comes under the oversight of the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government but acts largely independently – over how far to open it to scrutiny. Guy Shrubsole, author of Who Owns England?, urged people to get involved.

items.title: American Airlines hikes annual fees on rewards cards for first time since 2018
items.summary: American Airlines joined other airlines and banks in raising their airline credit card fee for one of their major cards.
items.body: American Airlines is raising the annual fee for two of its rewards credit cards for the first time since 2018 and adding new benefits like a TSA PreCheck credit and points from spending on hotels. The fee on the Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard will go up to $150 a year from $99. That is the first hike since 2018, when it raised the fee from $95 to $99, an airline spokeswoman said. The Citi AAdvantage Business Mastercard will also have a fee increase and will now cost $150 a year. Airlines and their bank partners have been steadily raising fees on rewards credit cards. Those cards generate billions of dollars a year for airlines, which make money when miles are sold to banks, which then give them to customers. American's move, announced Tuesday, follows similar increases by rivals such as United Airlines .
